Nursing progress note – Respiratory Medicine

Patient: phoebe-marie ahmad
DOB: 17 January 1986
Date: 1 Apr 2023
Documented by: daryle williamson

Admitted with infectious gastroenteritis. Ongoing loose stools and intermittent vomiting with abdominal cramps. HARDEEP HUGHES visited this afternoon and reports that the patient was managing small amounts of fluid at home before admission.

Observations stable: temperature 37.4°C, pulse 92 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO₂ 98% on air. Alert and answering appropriately. Mouth slightly dry; peripheral perfusion satisfactory. Abdomen soft, with mild generalised cramping on palpation and no guarding. Passed two watery stools during the shift and vomited once after attempting a larger drink.

Oral rehydration solution offered frequently in small volumes. Ondansetron given as required with good effect; no further vomiting for the remainder of the shift. Tolerated half a bowl of soup and several sips of water. Mobilising independently to the bathroom, though advised to call for assistance if dizzy. Stool chart and fluid balance maintained. Enhanced hand hygiene and contact precautions continued.

Assessment: gastrointestinal losses ongoing, with mild dehydration risk. Intake may improve with hydration, and this will be encouraged gradually rather than with large volumes. No current respiratory compromise.

Escalation: covering medical team to review if unable to retain fluids, urine output falls, abdominal pain becomes localised or severe, or observations deteriorate. Consider blood tests and intravenous fluids if oral replacement remains inadequate.

Plan for next shift: continue oral rehydration solution little and often, administer ondansetron as required, monitor stool/vomit frequency, urine output and observations, and review fluid balance with the nurse in charge.

Patient: Z. Herbert
MRN: 018703/98
Occupation: University lecturer
Seen at: Medical Centre Raf Cranwell
Clinician: DEVI CLAY

Reason for review
Review of deteriorating mood and response to sertraline.

History
Reports approximately six weeks of persistently low mood, with marked loss of interest in usual activities and reduced motivation. Sleep is disturbed by waking at around 04:00 and being unable to return to sleep. Appetite reduced, with no reported weight change. Describes fatigue, poor concentration and increasing difficulty managing routine tasks at work. Has been taking sertraline 50 mg once daily as prescribed for the last four weeks; mild nausea during the first week has settled. No symptoms suggestive of mania, psychosis or panic attacks.

Has felt more tearful for 3 days, in the context of a recent increase in workload, but denies alcohol excess or recreational drug use. No previous psychiatric admission. No current contact with secondary mental health services.

Risk assessment
Acknowledges occasional thoughts that life feels burdensome but denies thoughts of ending life, plans, intent or preparatory acts. No thoughts of harming anyone else. Protective factors include supportive family, responsibility for a pet and willingness to seek help. Agrees to contact the GP surgery, NHS 111 or A&E if suicidal thoughts develop or safety becomes difficult to maintain.

Examination
Engaged appropriately throughout, with reduced eye contact and subdued affect. Speech normal in rate and volume. Thought form coherent; no delusional content elicited. Fully orientated. Insight and judgement intact. No acute physical concerns reported.

Assessment
Major depressive episode with persistent low mood, anhedonia, early-morning waking and functional impairment. Partial response to sertraline after four weeks. Current risk assessed as low, with no suicidal intent or plan.

Plan
• Increase sertraline to 100 mg once daily, provided tolerated.
• Discussed expected onset of benefit, common adverse effects and avoiding abrupt discontinuation.
• Signposted to NHS Talking Therapies and encouraged graded activity, regular meals and a consistent sleep routine.
• Safety-netting discussed; seek urgent help via NHS 111 or emergency department if risk escalates.
• Follow-up with the GP in two weeks to review mood, sleep, adherence and suicidal ideation; earlier appointment if worsening.

Signed by DEVI CLAY at Medical Centre Raf Cranwell.

Nursing progress and handover note
NHS number: 0003264379
Date: 6th August 2021
Patient: Kimon J.
DOB: 26 Aug 1954

Admitted with community-acquired pneumonia, coded SNOMED CT 233604007. Productive cough continues, sputum yellow-green but no haemoptysis. Reports sharp right-sided pleuritic pain on deep inspiration, 4/10 at rest and 6/10 when coughing. Fever earlier in the shift; currently feels less chilled following treatment.

Observations at 18:30: temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm regular, respirations 22/min, BP 118/68 mmHg, oxygen saturations 94% on air. Alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences. Chest sounds reduced with coarse crackles at the right base. No acute increase in work of breathing.

Amoxicillin administered as prescribed; no rash, wheeze or other reaction observed. Paracetamol given for fever and pleuritic discomfort, with good effect: pain reduced to 2/10 and temperature settling. Encouraged regular fluids and small, frequent meals. Took approximately 900 mL orally during shift and ate half of lunch and most of an evening sandwich. Sputum pot provided; sample not yet produced.

Mobilised to bathroom with one staff member and walking frame. Mild breathlessness on return, resolved after seated rest. Falls precautions maintained: call bell within reach, non-slip footwear in place, bed in lowest position. Patient understands to request assistance before mobilising.

Daughter, NAFISHA SUTCLIFFE, updated at the bedside with the patient’s consent. Patient remains concerned about managing stairs at home; reassurance given and occupational therapy review to be considered if mobility does not improve.

Escalate promptly for increasing respiratory effort, new confusion, persistent fever, oxygen saturations below 92% on air, chest pain not relieved by prescribed analgesia, or inability to maintain oral intake. Contact medical team if observations deteriorate; consider repeat NEWS2 assessment and oxygen prescription review.

Plan for next shift: continue observations and respiratory assessment, administer antibiotics and analgesia on time, encourage fluids, coughing and deep-breathing exercises, record sputum, and supervise mobilisation. Handover completed to andreana johnston, nurse in charge.

LABORATORY REPORT
NHS number: 000 649 5673

Patient: Omari
Report/accession ID: 03067876
Requesting service: THE ROYAL VICTORIA INFIRMARY
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA; serum
Clinical details: Painless cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Suspected Hodgkin lymphoma. Supportive care pending tissue diagnosis.

HAEMATOLOGY

Haemoglobin: 108 g/L (120–160)
White cell count: 12.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0)
Neutrophils: 9.6 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5)
Lymphocytes: 1.7 ×10⁹/L (1.0–4.0)
Platelets: 468 ×10⁹/L (150–400)
Mean cell volume (MCV): 86 fL (80–100)
Mean cell haemoglobin: 29 pg (27–33)
Red cell distribution width: 15.2% (11.5–14.5)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 72 mm/hour (0–20)

BIOCHEMISTRY

C-reactive protein: 64 mg/L (<5)
Lactate dehydrogenase: 318 U/L (120–250)
Urate: 0.39 mmol/L (0.15–0.35)
Creatinine: 74 micromol/L (45–90)
Estimated GFR: >90 mL/min/1.73 m²
Alanine aminotransferase: 22 U/L (5–35)
Alkaline phosphatase: 126 U/L (30–130)
Bilirubin: 9 micromol/L (0–21)
Albumin: 32 g/L (35–50)
Calcium, adjusted: 2.35 mmol/L (2.20–2.60)

INTERPRETATION

Mild normocytic anaemia with neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis and thrombocytosis. ESR and C-reactive protein are substantially raised. There is a modest increase in lactate dehydrogenase and urate, with hypoalbuminaemia. Renal and hepatic indices are currently satisfactory.

CLINICAL COMMENT

The inflammatory profile is compatible with the reported constitutional symptoms but is non-specific. These results neither confirm nor exclude Hodgkin lymphoma. Urgent tissue diagnosis, including appropriate histopathological and immunophenotypic assessment of an accessible lymph node, remains required. Consider baseline tumour lysis risk assessment before systemic treatment, with repeat urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium and renal function if treatment is commenced. Correlate with imaging and haematology review.

Current medication entry: supportive care pending tissue diagnosis; no active antineoplastic treatment recorded.

Follow-up: Haematology review booked for 8 July 2022. Please contact the laboratory if additional pre-treatment investigations are required.

Validated and electronically authorised by: harriette kane
Laboratory report status: Final

Rheumatology referral

Date: 21/06/2028
To: Rheumatology Service

Re: AOUS SHAW
Report/accession ID: 07394047

Dear Rheumatology Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of AOUS SHAW, who has developed a clinically significant flare of rheumatoid arthritis despite ongoing disease-modifying treatment. The specific questions are whether treatment escalation is indicated and whether the current symptoms reflect active inflammatory disease rather than mechanical hand pain or medication-related adverse effects.

Over recent weeks, the patient has experienced increasing morning stiffness, now lasting approximately two hours, with painful swelling affecting both hands. The metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints are particularly troublesome, with reduced grip strength and difficulty opening jars and fastening clothing. Fatigue has also become prominent and is limiting usual daily activities. There has been no reported fever, recent infection, weight loss or new rash. The patient denies ocular pain, persistent diarrhoea and symptoms suggestive of another systemic inflammatory condition.

On review, there is visible soft-tissue swelling and tenderness across several bilateral MCP and PIP joints, with reduced flexion because of pain. The wrists are uncomfortable on movement, although there is no clear large-joint effusion. There is no dactylitis or proximal muscle weakness. The patient appears tired but clinically well, with no evidence of acute infection. Recent blood results show a raised inflammatory response in keeping with the examination; renal and hepatic profiles remain suitable for continuation of current medication. A contemporaneous hand radiograph has not demonstrated an acute fracture; the formal report is linked to the above accession identifier.

Current treatment is methotrexate 15 mg once weekly with folic acid as prescribed, together with naproxen for symptomatic relief. The patient reports adherence and has not knowingly omitted methotrexate doses. Naproxen has provided only partial benefit. Gastrointestinal tolerance has been acceptable, and there has been no reported mouth ulceration, unusual bruising or breathlessness. We have reinforced that methotrexate must be taken weekly rather than daily and have advised the patient to seek advice promptly if infection develops.

Pending your review, I have advised continuation of the existing regimen, with monitoring blood tests through primary care and avoidance of over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicines in addition to naproxen. Please consider whether a short corticosteroid bridge, optimisation of methotrexate, or commencement of an alternative conventional or biological disease-modifying agent would be appropriate. Assessment of disease activity and repeat imaging may also be helpful.

Thank you for seeing this patient. Please send your recommendations to ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH.

Yours faithfully,

R. Baines
Referring clinician
ROYAL INFIRMARY OF EDINBURGH

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: B. Hobbs
Report/accession ID: 08538226
Specimen: Serum, collected during assessment for reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake.
Clinical indication: Acute kidney injury; receiving intravenous sodium chloride with temporary medication hold.

Results
Urea: 18.6 mmol/L (reference interval 2.5–7.8) — raised
Creatinine: 286 µmol/L (reference interval 45–90) — raised
eGFR: 19 mL/min/1.73 m² — reduced; interpret cautiously in acute change
Sodium: 138 mmol/L (133–146) — within range
Potassium: 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.3) — within range
Bicarbonate: 21 mmol/L (22–29) — mildly reduced
Chloride: 104 mmol/L (98–107) — within range
CRP: 12 mg/L (<5) — mildly raised
Haemoglobin: 126 g/L (115–160) — within range

Interpretation
The markedly increased creatinine and urea are consistent with significant acute kidney injury. The preserved potassium and near-normal sodium are reassuring at this time, although renal function remains substantially impaired. Mildly reduced bicarbonate may reflect reduced renal acid excretion. Clinical correlation is required, including fluid balance, blood pressure, urine output and assessment for obstruction or sepsis.

Comment
Continue careful assessment of response to intravenous sodium chloride, avoiding fluid overload. Review nephrotoxic medicines and the temporary medication hold before reintroduction. Repeat U&E and creatinine promptly, with urgent escalation if urine output falls further, potassium rises, breathlessness develops or the patient becomes clinically unwell. Urinalysis and renal ultrasound should be considered if the cause is not clear or improvement is not seen.

Planned clinical review: 6 Apr 2026 (in about 9 weeks). Earlier renal review is indicated if biochemical recovery is incomplete.

Validated and reported by: J. PRIESTLEY, laboratory physician
GMC professional identifier: 0952126

NHS number: 000 583 0444

Patient: Kathir Shaw
DOB: 18/09/1928
Address: 34 East Duck Lees Lane, Hackney, E9 5AA
Contact: 07700 900035

Presenting complaint: 24-hour history of profuse watery diarrhoea, four episodes of vomiting and intermittent central abdominal cramps. Sibling reports reduced oral intake. No blood or mucus in stool. No recent antibiotics, foreign travel or known sick contacts. Passing urine, though less frequently than usual. Abdominal pain currently 5/10.

Safety-netted regarding persistent vomiting, inability to pass urine, worsening/localised pain, fever, blood in stool or collapse. Infection-control advice provided.

Disposition: Discharged home with sibling; GP review if not improving within 48 hours.

Signed: Dr Vedant FISHER, MBBS

Discharge summary
NHS number: 0009692453

Patient: K. Golding
Discharging service: ULSTER HOSPITAL
Report/accession ID: 012414516

Reason for admission
Admitted with several days of reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake. The presentation was consistent with acute kidney injury, most likely related to reduced circulating volume in the context of inadequate intake. There was no reported flank pain, dysuria or visible haematuria.

Assessment and hospital course
On arrival, the patient appeared clinically dry, with concentrated urine and a raised serum creatinine compared with the previous primary care result. Urinalysis showed no significant blood or protein. Renal ultrasound demonstrated kidneys of preserved size with no hydronephrosis or other evidence of urinary tract obstruction. The case was reviewed with the renal team, who advised conservative management and monitoring.

Intravenous sodium chloride was given with careful fluid-balance assessment. Urine output improved during admission and the patient was able to maintain oral fluids before discharge. The temporary medication hold was maintained while renal function recovered; the patient has been advised not to restart the withheld medicines until reviewed by the GP or renal team. No dialysis was required. Electrolytes remained suitable for discharge, and the discharge blood tests showed a clear improvement in renal function, although not yet confirmed to be fully back to baseline.

Genetics review
The clinical genetics team considered whether an inherited predisposition to renal disease required further assessment. There was no indication for urgent genetic testing during this admission. The patient was advised that any further investigation would depend on repeat renal results, personal history and relevant family history. A copy of this summary will be available to the treating clinicians.

Problem list
• Acute kidney injury, improving with rehydration
• Reduced oral intake and oliguria, resolved
• Temporary hold of regular medicines pending renal review
• Need for repeat renal monitoring

Discharge advice
Drink regularly unless otherwise instructed. Seek urgent medical attention via A&E if urine output falls again, vomiting prevents drinking, breathlessness develops, or there is increasing drowsiness or confusion. Avoid over-the-counter anti-inflammatory painkillers unless specifically authorised by a clinician. Please arrange a GP blood test and medication review promptly after discharge.

Follow-up
Renal function and electrolytes should be repeated through the GP surgery. Clinical genetics follow-up is planned in about 7 weeks, with earlier review if renal function deteriorates or further concerning family history becomes available.

Discharging clinician: D. Pickering, GMC number GMC 0399628

Clinical genetics laboratory report

Patient: F. Kennedy
Patient identifier (MRN): 063073971
Clinical age: 87 y/o
Specimen: EDTA blood
Collection/report date: 10th April 2035
Request: Investigation of diabetes mellitus with thirst, fatigue and frequent urination. Current treatment recorded as metformin and atorvastatin. Family history and the identity of the ordering clinician were not provided.

Test performed: Targeted analysis of a diabetes mellitus gene panel, including GCK, HNF1A, HNF4A, INS and selected syndromic diabetes genes. Sequencing and copy-number analysis undertaken using validated clinical laboratory methods.

Result: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analysed. This result does not exclude a genetic contribution to diabetes, variants outside the regions examined, or a non-genetic cause. Variant of uncertain significance: none reported.

Interpretation: The findings do not support a molecular diagnosis of monogenic diabetes on this assay. Correlate with phenotype, age at onset, treatment history, body habitus and three-generation family history. Routine diabetes care should continue under the treating clinical team; metformin and atorvastatin should not be altered on the basis of this report alone.

Recommendation: Review glycaemic indices and urine testing clinically. If atypical features or a strong multigenerational history emerge, genetics review may be appropriate in about 3 weeks, with consideration of broader testing after counselling.

Clinical genetics laboratory clinician

Discharge Summary
NHS number: 000 276 8284

Patient: V. Myers
MRN: H4741379
Responsible service: Clinical Genetics, Ulster Hospital

Reason for admission
Presented via the emergency department with a 48-hour history of frequent watery diarrhoea, vomiting and intermittent abdominal cramps. History was obtained from the patient and their partner. There was no reported blood in the stool, persistent severe abdominal pain or recent overseas travel.

Key findings
On arrival, the patient was mildly dehydrated but haemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination showed mild, diffuse discomfort without guarding or rebound tenderness. Blood tests demonstrated a modest rise in urea consistent with reduced oral intake; inflammatory markers were not significantly elevated. Stool testing was sent and did not identify a bacterial pathogen or Clostridioides difficile. The overall picture was consistent with self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis.

Hospital course
The patient received intravenous crystalloid initially, followed by oral rehydration solution as vomiting settled. Ondansetron was given as required, with good effect. Diarrhoeal frequency reduced during observation and the patient subsequently tolerated fluids and light meals. Renal function improved on repeat testing. There was no indication for antibiotic treatment.

The abdominal cramps and nausea may improve with hydration. Advice was provided regarding hand hygiene and avoiding food preparation for others until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. The partner was present for discharge discussions with the patient’s agreement.

Discharge medication
• Oral rehydration solution, prepared and taken according to the packet instructions.
• Ondansetron as required for nausea, supplied for short-term use.

Condition at discharge
Alert, clinically euvolaemic and managing oral fluids. No abdominal tenderness requiring further inpatient assessment. Discharged home with partner.

Follow-up and safety-netting
No routine hospital follow-up is required. Please contact the GP surgery if symptoms have not substantially improved, or if diarrhoea persists beyond the expected course. Attend A&E urgently for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, markedly reduced urine output, blood in stool, severe or localised abdominal pain, or new confusion.

Discharging clinician: Aisleen Goddard, GMC identifier GMC 0869345

Re: Mahdia CHADWICK

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient, who has developed a major depressive episode with persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities and early-morning waking. Symptoms have been present for several weeks and are now affecting day-to-day functioning and communication with their partner.

At review, Mahdia CHADWICK appeared subdued, with reduced spontaneous speech but good engagement throughout the consultation. They described little pleasure in routine activities and waking well before the intended time, after which they are unable to return to sleep. Appetite is variable and concentration is reduced. There is no history in the available record to suggest mania, psychosis or problematic alcohol or illicit drug use.

The patient has been taking sertraline 50 mg once daily, with adherence reported as good. They have received brief supportive advice regarding sleep routine, activity scheduling and maintaining contact with their partner. Despite this, the depressive symptoms remain clinically significant. They denied current thoughts, plans or intent to harm themselves, although a full safety discussion was completed. Their partner is aware of the deterioration and is providing support at home.

Assessment

Major depressive episode with prominent anhedonia and biological sleep disturbance, with incomplete response to initial primary-care management. No psychotic features or current suicidal intent elicited today.

Request

Please assess the diagnosis and severity, advise on optimisation of pharmacological treatment and consider whether structured psychological therapy or other secondary-care input would be appropriate. Advice regarding ongoing risk monitoring would also be appreciated. The patient has been advised to seek urgent help via A&E or emergency services if suicidal thoughts, intent or inability to remain safe develop.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Arista Field, MBBS

Patient: kobey iqbal

The historical imaging correspondence was reviewed by the consultant neurologist; no acute neurological deficit was identified. Follow-up has been arranged for 19 February 1988, with earlier GP review if pain control is inadequate or function deteriorates.

MOLECULAR GENETICS REPORT

Patient: Zelah RHODES
MRN: 067 398 114
Date of report: 27/06/2035
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer; predictive testing requested following counselling. Sibling reported to carry a familial BRCA1 variant. Cancer-risk concern documented.

Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA.
Test: Germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis.
Patient context: a 50-year-old White female patient with no current treatment.

Result:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG detected in the heterozygous state. This is a pathogenic variant associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility.

Interpretation:
The finding confirms a germline BRCA1 pathogenic variant. The result is consistent with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk and should be interpreted alongside the reported family history. This is a predictive result where clinically unaffected status is not inferred from the laboratory finding.

Clinical comment:
Please refer to the regional clinical genetics service for formal result disclosure, individualised surveillance planning and discussion of risk-reducing options. Cascade testing should be offered to eligible relatives after appropriate counselling. The laboratory cannot determine the presence or absence of cancer from this result. Genetic counselling is recommended before testing additional family members.

Analytical limitations:
This assay does not exclude pathogenic variants in other cancer-predisposition genes or deep intronic/regulatory regions not covered by the method. Variant classification may change as evidence develops; the result should be reviewed if relevant clinical or family-history information changes.

Validated and reported by:
halima-sadia ahmed
Laboratory clinician

No treatment is prescribed by the laboratory.

Thank you for attending the respiratory clinic with your adult child. We discussed the episodes of sudden palpitations, chest tightness and an intense fear of dying. The most recent episode has been present for 3 days in total, with symptoms rising quickly and then easing. You have not described exertional breathlessness, productive cough or wheeze, and there is no history to suggest an acute chest infection.

Your examination today was reassuring, with clear breath sounds and no signs of respiratory distress. The pattern is most consistent with panic attacks and over-breathing rather than asthma or another primary lung condition. We discussed how rapid upper-chest breathing can amplify tingling, tightness and the sensation that something dangerous is happening.

Practise when calm as well as during symptoms. A written breathing plan was provided. We recommend discussing talking therapy, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, with your GP if these episodes continue or begin to affect daily activities.

No respiratory medication is indicated at present. Seek urgent help via 999 if chest pain is persistent, occurs with collapse, or is accompanied by marked breathlessness. Otherwise, please contact your GP if the episodes change or become more frequent.

We will review you on 2 December 1988. Your preferred contact detail is emie-rose.o'neill80@yahoo.co.uk.

Patient: sepehr arnold
MRN: MRN-06977374
Referring organisation: Aberdeen Royal Infirmary

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with progressive symptoms consistent with osteoarthritis of the knee. The specific question is whether specialist review and consideration of intra-articular treatment or operative planning would be appropriate, given persistent pain and declining mobility despite conservative measures.

The patient reports several months of activity-related knee pain, with morning stiffness and difficulty walking on stairs and uneven ground. There has been no preceding significant injury, locking episode or systemic upset. They attended the emergency department because of an increase in pain and reduced function. Current pain score is 5/10. Examination demonstrated an antalgic gait, medial joint-line tenderness and reduced flexion, without erythema, appreciable effusion or neurovascular deficit.

Plain radiographs obtained during the attendance show compartmental joint-space narrowing with marginal osteophyte formation, in keeping with degenerative change. There are no acute bony findings. The presentation and imaging are therefore most compatible with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis rather than an acute traumatic process or septic joint.

Management to date has included advice regarding pacing, use of a stick when required, paracetamol and topical ibuprofen. The patient remains limited in usual activities and would value discussion of further non-operative options, including physiotherapy and injection therapy, and whether orthopaedic opinion is indicated.

The patient was accompanied by a friend, who assisted with the history. Please review and advise on ongoing management.

Yours faithfully,

chimdi foster

Referral to Neurology

Patient: T. Humphrey
Address: 60 Buckstone Gate, Newport-on-Tay, DD6 8AA
Occupation: bus driver

Dear Colleague,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with persistent low back pain and left-sided shooting leg pain, associated with intermittent paraesthesia. The clinical question is whether the symptoms represent lumbar radiculopathy requiring imaging, specialist intervention or physiotherapy-led management, and whether there are features to suggest a more proximal neurological process.

Symptoms began gradually and have continued despite activity modification. Pain is worse with prolonged sitting and forward flexion, with occasional nocturnal discomfort. There is no reported sphincter disturbance or saddle sensory change. The patient remains independently mobile but is limiting work and usual exercise.

On examination, lumbar flexion is reduced by pain. Straight-leg raise reproduces posterior leg pain on the affected side. Lower-limb power is preserved, with no clear focal sensory loss elicited today; reflexes are symmetrical. No systemic features were identified. There has been no recent trauma.

Initial management has comprised naproxen with food and paracetamol, together with advice regarding pacing and gentle mobility exercises. Benefit has been incomplete. No spinal imaging has yet been undertaken. The opinion of a consultant neurologist would be useful if the distribution or paraesthesia warrants further neurological investigation.

Please advise on the need for MRI and any recommended medication or rehabilitation pathway. The patient has been asked to seek urgent review for new weakness, bladder or bowel disturbance, or saddle numbness.

Follow-up appointment planned for 24/06/1996.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Sadaa Hasan, MBBS

Continue supportive care with paracetamol as required, encourage fluids, and seek urgent review for increasing drowsiness, persistent vomiting, mastoid swelling or clinical deterioration. NHS number: 000 634 1447

Patient: heny fisher
DOB: 12 Nov 2017
MRN: 075545705
Legal guardian: Eiryn Sanders
Discharging organisation: ULSTER HOSPITAL

Reason for admission
Presented with 24 hours of frequent vomiting and watery diarrhoea, with reduced urine output and poor oral intake. Legal guardian reported no blood in stool and no persistent abdominal pain. Admitted for assessment and rehydration.

Assessment and results
Initially mildly dehydrated: dry lips, reduced tears and delayed capillary refill. Abdomen soft, non-distended and non-tender. No clinical features of meningism or sepsis. Blood glucose normal. Urea and electrolytes remained within acceptable limits for age; no indication for intravenous antibiotics or imaging. Stool sampling was not required during this admission.

Hospital course
Managed with oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts, with supportive care and close fluid balance monitoring. Vomiting settled and oral intake gradually improved. Urine output returned to usual pattern. Diarrhoea continued intermittently but was less frequent by discharge; nausea may improve with hydration. No further clinical evidence of significant dehydration. Guardian remained with the child and was involved in care and discharge planning.

Problem list
• Acute gastroenteritis
• Mild dehydration, resolved
• Vomiting and diarrhoea, improving
• Reduced urine output, resolved

Discharge plan
Discharge home with legal guardian. Continue oral rehydration solution regularly, particularly after loose stools or vomiting, and offer usual feeds/food in small portions as tolerated. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal medicines unless advised by a clinician. Supportive care only; no new prescription medicines.

Return to A&E or contact the GP urgently if the child becomes unusually drowsy, cannot keep fluids down, passes very little urine, develops blood in the stool, severe abdominal pain, breathing difficulty or worsening fever. GP review if symptoms have not clearly improved over the next few days. Discharge advice discussed with and understood by Eiryn Sanders.

SITUATION
A&E handover, 15 Jan 2024: Marnie-Rose Ritchie with acute left flank pain, dysuria and rigors for 3 days. Partner D. LYONS present and provides collateral history. Referred from Cardiff Royal Infirmary.

BACKGROUND
No known renal disease documented. Reports nausea but no vomiting. No recent admission or urinary instrumentation. Medication history checked: cefuroxime and paracetamol.

ASSESSMENT / CONCERN
Febrile and tachycardic on arrival; BP maintained, alert and perfusing. Left renal angle tenderness, mild suprapubic discomfort. No peritonism. Sepsis screen triggered. Working diagnosis: acute pyelonephritis; consider obstructed infected system if pain worsens or renal function abnormal.

INVESTIGATIONS
Urine dip positive for leucocytes and nitrites, blood present. Urine culture sent before antibiotics. FBC, U&Es, CRP, lactate and blood cultures requested. ECG completed for baseline; no acute ischaemic change. Renal tract imaging to be considered if poor response or obstruction suspected.

ACTIONS / PLAN
IV access established; blood cultures taken. Paracetamol given, oral fluids encouraged, IV crystalloid if unable to maintain intake. Start empiric IV cefuroxime as prescribed, pending cultures and local antimicrobial guidance. Monitor observations and urine output; repeat lactate if initially raised. Senior review after results.

DISPOSITION / SAFETY NET
Admit for IV antibiotics and observation if persistent fever, vomiting, hypotension or abnormal renal function. If clinically improved and suitable for oral treatment, discuss discharge with GP follow-up and clear return advice. Documented by jaevon atkinson.

Patient: skailar proszek
DOB: Feb 25, 1965

skailar proszek was admitted from the emergency department for sudden breathlessness, sharp pleuritic chest pain, and persistent tachycardia. Initial oxygen saturation was low on room air, and CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute bilateral pulmonary emboli without evidence of hemodynamic collapse. Lower-extremity venous ultrasound showed a nonocclusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein. Troponin was minimally elevated but remained stable on repeat testing, and echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function with no significant right ventricular strain.

The patient initially required supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula. Anticoagulation was started with apixaban after discussion of bleeding risk, medication adherence, and the importance of avoiding missed doses. There was no indication for thrombolysis or catheter-directed intervention. Pleuritic discomfort improved with acetaminophen, and the patient did not develop recurrent syncope, hypotension, or increasing oxygen needs. A medication reconciliation was completed with the patient and kaiyer pessagno, who participated by telephone. The patient reported no prior history of major bleeding.

On the day of discharge, the patient was breathing comfortably without supplemental oxygen at rest and with ambulation. Heart rate had improved, and blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg. Lung examination was clear, and there was no new leg swelling. The patient was alert, able to explain the anticoagulation plan, and considered medically stable for discharge home.

Assessment and plan:
1. Acute pulmonary embolism with associated left popliteal deep venous thrombosis, clinically improved. Continue apixaban 10 mg twice daily to complete the initial treatment phase, then decrease to 5 mg twice daily as instructed on the prescription. Duration of therapy will be reassessed in follow-up.
2. Pleuritic chest pain, improving. Use acetaminophen as needed. Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless specifically approved by a clinician.
3. Hypoxemia, resolved. Supplemental oxygen is not required at discharge.

The patient was instructed to seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, fainting, new or severe chest pain, coughing or vomiting blood, black stools, uncontrolled bleeding, or a significant head injury. The patient should avoid activities with a high risk of trauma and should notify all healthcare professionals that apixaban is being taken.

Follow-up with primary care and anticoagulation review is scheduled for 2029-01-20. The patient may contact the care team using skailar.proszek52@att.net for routine medication questions. Discharge instructions were reviewed verbally, and the patient stated understanding.

SSN: 666 85 9708

Patient: skailar proszek
DOB: Feb 25, 1965

skailar proszek was admitted from the emergency department for sudden breathlessness, sharp pleuritic chest pain, and persistent tachycardia. Initial oxygen saturation was low on room air, and CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute bilateral pulmonary emboli without evidence of hemodynamic collapse. Lower-extremity venous ultrasound showed a nonocclusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein. Troponin was minimally elevated but remained stable on repeat testing, and echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function with no significant right ventricular strain.

The patient initially required supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula. Anticoagulation was started with apixaban after discussion of bleeding risk, medication adherence, and the importance of avoiding missed doses. There was no indication for thrombolysis or catheter-directed intervention. Pleuritic discomfort improved with acetaminophen, and the patient did not develop recurrent syncope, hypotension, or increasing oxygen needs. A medication reconciliation was completed with the patient and kaiyer pessagno, who participated by telephone. The patient reported no prior history of major bleeding.

On the day of discharge, the patient was breathing comfortably without supplemental oxygen at rest and with ambulation. Heart rate had improved, and blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg. Lung examination was clear, and there was no new leg swelling. The patient was alert, able to explain the anticoagulation plan, and considered medically stable for discharge home.

Assessment and plan:
1. Acute pulmonary embolism with associated left popliteal deep venous thrombosis, clinically improved. Continue apixaban 10 mg twice daily to complete the initial treatment phase, then decrease to 5 mg twice daily as instructed on the prescription. Duration of therapy will be reassessed in follow-up.
2. Pleuritic chest pain, improving. Use acetaminophen as needed. Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless specifically approved by a clinician.
3. Hypoxemia, resolved. Supplemental oxygen is not required at discharge.

The patient was instructed to seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, fainting, new or severe chest pain, coughing or vomiting blood, black stools, uncontrolled bleeding, or a significant head injury. The patient should avoid activities with a high risk of trauma and should notify all healthcare professionals that apixaban is being taken.

Follow-up with primary care and anticoagulation review is scheduled for 2029-01-20. The patient may contact the care team using skailar.proszek52@att.net for routine medication questions. Discharge instructions were reviewed verbally, and the patient stated understanding.

Date: 2025-03-15
Patient: FORREST GATES
DOB: October 5th, 1947
Primary clinician: nasli abro

Assessment: Older adult admitted with COPD exacerbation. Reports increased breathlessness with activity, chest tightness, and fatigue. Productive cough with thick yellow-green sputum. Audible expiratory wheeze bilaterally, diminished bases. RR 24/min, SpO2 91% on room air; improved to 94% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. HR 96, BP 138/76, oral temp 99.1°F. Interventions: Administered albuterol inhaler per MAR with spacer; wheeze decreased and patient reported easier breathing. Prednisone and doxycycline given as ordered, tolerated without nausea. Encouraged fluids and coughing/deep-breathing exercises. Sputum specimen obtained, moderate amount, purulent. Intake limited at breakfast, approximately 40%; accepted half a protein shake. Urine output adequate. No bowel movement this shift.

Risk/escalation: Oxygen continued at 2 L/min; titrate per order and monitor for worsening hypoxia or increased work of breathing. Provider nasli abro notified of persistent exertional dyspnea and sputum color; no new orders at this time. Emergency contact/daughter: Jeter Rail.

Next shift: Reassess respiratory status and response to bronchodilator, monitor SpO2 and sputum, encourage mobility only with assistance, continue fall precautions, hydration, and medication schedule. Notify provider for SpO2 below ordered goal, confusion, inability to speak, or respiratory distress.

Clinical Genetics Referral
SSN: 666-20-0263

Patient: H. Mcevers
MRN: 0972902
Home address: 684 Colorado Ave, Gilcrest, CO 80623
Reason for referral: Evaluation for possible hereditary Parkinson disease and counseling regarding familial risk.

Clinical history: The patient has an established diagnosis of Parkinson disease previously assessed by Neurology. Symptoms began with a predominantly right-sided resting tremor and have progressed to bradykinesia and muscular rigidity. There is no reported early cognitive decline, seizures, developmental concern, or known atypical parkinsonism. The patient remains independent with basic activities but notes slower dressing, reduced handwriting size, and occasional difficulty initiating gait. Spouse provided additional history and is concerned about implications for biological relatives.

Current treatment: Carbidopa-levodopa is prescribed through primary care following prior neurologic evaluation. The patient reports partial benefit and no dyskinesias, hallucinations, or symptomatic orthostasis. No prior genetic testing is documented. Family history is incomplete; the patient recalls a relative with late-life tremor but does not know the diagnosis.

Examination today: Alert and conversant. Mild hypomimia, bilateral upper-extremity rigidity, and decrement with finger tapping, greater on the right. Resting tremor is intermittent. Gait is slow with reduced arm swing; no freezing observed in the office.

Clinical question/request: Please assess whether the presentation warrants a hereditary Parkinson disease panel or targeted testing, review the limitations and potential implications of results, and provide pretest and post-test genetic counseling. Please advise whether additional family-history documentation or testing of an affected relative would be more informative. Follow-up review is scheduled for April 7th, 2012.

Referring clinician: Brenham Gledhill, MD

Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: Yuriy Horii
Report/accession ID: 01829112
Presenting concern: Flank pain, dysuria, and rigors

Yuriy Horii presented to the emergency department with two days of worsening left flank pain and burning with urination, followed by shaking chills this evening. The patient reports urinary frequency and nausea but no vomiting, diarrhea, vaginal symptoms, or visible blood in the urine. jyair deziel, the patient’s spouse, provided additional history and confirms no recent urinary procedure or known kidney stone. Current medications include acetaminophen for pain and cefuroxime, which was started before arrival.

On examination, the patient appeared uncomfortable but alert and appropriately interactive. Temperature was elevated, with mild tachycardia and stable blood pressure. There was left costovertebral angle tenderness and mild suprapubic discomfort without guarding or rebound. Lungs were clear, and there was no rash or focal neurologic deficit. Peripheral perfusion was preserved.

Urinalysis showed marked leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, pyuria, and microscopic hematuria. CBC demonstrated leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance. Metabolic testing showed preserved renal function and no significant electrolyte abnormality. Serum lactate was not elevated. A urine culture was obtained before antibiotics. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or obstructing calculus. The result was filed under report/accession ID 01829112.

Assessment: Findings are most consistent with acute pyelonephritis. There is no current evidence of septic shock, obstructive uropathy, or peritonitis. The patient tolerated oral intake in the ED and had improved pain and nausea after treatment.

Plan: Cefuroxime was continued, with dosing reviewed for renal function, and acetaminophen was recommended for fever and discomfort. The patient received intravenous fluids and an initial parenteral antibiotic dose while awaiting culture results. Strict return precautions were provided for persistent fever, worsening pain, vomiting, confusion, fainting, or inability to take medication. The patient was discharged in stable condition with follow-up arranged through MOLOKAI GENERAL HOSPITAL on April 1st, 2022, in 15 days, or sooner if symptoms do not steadily improve.

Internal Medicine Consultation Note
SSN: 958962702

Patient: crockett mohawk
Contact: (212) 555-0130
Encounter date: 2026-03-13
Report/accession ID: A22Z60687
Clinical age group: 67 y/o
Source of history: Patient and spouse

Reason for consultation: Acute right first metatarsophalangeal joint pain with swelling and erythema.

History of present illness: The patient developed abrupt, severe pain at the base of the right great toe approximately 2 days ago. Symptoms progressed overnight, with marked tenderness, warmth, and difficulty bearing weight. The spouse reports no preceding trauma, laceration, or recent procedure. The patient denies fever, chills, calf pain, dysuria, or other new joint symptoms. There is no reported history of nephrolithiasis. Oral intake has been reduced because movement worsens the pain.

Medication review: Current treatment includes colchicine. The patient has also used naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food as previously instructed. No anticoagulant use was reported. Medication allergies were reviewed in the chart and discussed during the visit.

Examination: The patient is uncomfortable with ambulation but is alert and nontoxic appearing. The right first metatarsophalangeal joint demonstrates pronounced swelling, erythema, increased warmth, and exquisite focal tenderness. Active and passive range of motion are substantially limited by pain. No drainage, fluctuance, ulceration, streaking erythema, or proximal lymphangitic change is seen. The ankle and other examined joints are without synovitis. Distal sensation and capillary refill are intact. Temperature is not elevated in the office.

Impression: Findings are most consistent with an acute gout flare involving the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Septic arthritis is less likely given the absence of systemic illness or skin breakdown, but it remains an important exclusion if fever develops, symptoms rapidly worsen, or the response to treatment is inadequate. Cellulitis and traumatic synovitis are less favored.

Plan: Continue colchicine according to the established prescription and continue naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food if tolerated. Take naproxen with adequate hydration and discontinue it for melena, hematemesis, severe abdominal pain, or allergic symptoms. Avoid alcohol and high-purine meals during the flare. Rest, elevate, and apply intermittent ice. Serum urate, CBC, metabolic panel, and inflammatory markers will be obtained if symptoms persist or recur. Urgent ED evaluation is advised for fever, rapidly spreading redness, inability to move the joint, or systemic weakness. Follow-up with internal medicine is recommended after resolution to discuss urate-lowering prevention.

Emergency Department Cardiology Assessment

Patient: DARIANNY TIERRABLANCA
Arrival: Ambulance
Report/accession ID: 079260882
Treating organization: PAINTSVILLE ARH HOSPITAL

DARIANNY TIERRABLANCA presented with 10 hours of severe bilateral arm and leg pain extending into the lower back, consistent with prior sickle cell painful crises. The patient reported poor oral intake and dark urine since yesterday but denied chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, cough, abdominal pain, vomiting, or focal weakness. The patient’s sibling, parsa manship, accompanied them and provided additional history. Patient contact detail is listed as darianny.tierrablanca53@gmail.com.

On arrival, the patient appeared uncomfortable and mildly dry but was alert and cooperative. Temperature was 98.6°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Mucous membranes were dry. Cardiac examination showed mild tachycardia with regular rhythm and no murmur. Lungs were clear bilaterally without increased work of breathing. The abdomen was soft and nontender. There was diffuse tenderness of both upper and lower extremities and the lumbar paraspinal region without swelling, erythema, or focal joint abnormality. Distal pulses and sensation were intact. Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

Laboratory testing showed mild leukocytosis without left shift, hemoglobin near the patient’s reported baseline, normal platelet count, and mildly elevated reticulocyte count. Creatinine and electrolytes were within normal limits. Urinalysis showed concentrated urine without evidence of infection. A pregnancy test was negative. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Chest radiograph showed no acute cardiopulmonary process.

Assessment: Acute vaso-occlusive pain episode with clinical dehydration. There is no current evidence of acute chest syndrome, sepsis, stroke, or significant renal complication.

The patient received intravenous crystalloid, morphine with reassessment-guided repeat dosing, and oral fluids as tolerated. Pain improved substantially, heart rate normalized, and the patient was able to ambulate. Hematology was consulted through PAINTSVILLE ARH HOSPITAL, and admission was not felt necessary after clinical improvement.

Plan: Continue the patient’s established home pain regimen, maintain hydration, and follow up with hematology and primary care. Return immediately for fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, worsening pain, weakness, or inability to drink. Discharged home in stable condition with parsa manship.

Consider repeat electrolytes and urine ketones per provider plan.

Next shift: Reassess nausea, orthostatic symptoms, urine output, IV site, and oral tolerance. Continue fluids and antiemetic regimen as prescribed. Handoff completed by nurse, professional ID LIC24111767.

Reassess wound and vital signs, monitor glucose and medication response, maintain dressing, reinforce off-loading, and confirm follow-up instructions before disposition.

Dear Colleague,

I am referring Kennay T., who was evaluated in community pediatrics for acute otitis media with persistent ear pain, fever, and irritability. The patient, age 18 months, was brought by the parent, M. Tacoma, who reports disrupted sleep and reduced interest in meals since symptoms began. There has been no ear drainage, breathing difficulty, or concern for dehydration.

The family has been advised to encourage fluids and return promptly for worsening pain, persistent fever, drainage, or poor intake. Symptoms have not improved as expected, and I would appreciate your assessment regarding persistent middle-ear inflammation, hearing impact, and whether additional treatment or short-term follow-up is indicated.

Assessment: Acute otitis media with ongoing otalgia and fever despite supportive management.

Plan: Please evaluate and advise regarding otoscopic findings, hearing assessment if appropriate, and further management. Primary care follow-up is planned in about 3 weeks, or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Sincerely,

Relena Duzan
Community Pediatrics
Freeport

Employer: Toledo Housing Authority
Home address: 707 Umpqua Ave, Plush, OR 97637
Contact: (212) 555-0112

Reason for visit: Evaluation of intermittent palpitations and chest awareness.

The patient reports several months of persistent worry with difficulty “turning off” thoughts at night. Sleep has been poor, and there is frequent neck and shoulder muscle tension. Over the past several weeks, episodes of a faster heartbeat have occurred mainly at rest or before work meetings, without syncope or exertional limitation. Mild chest tightness has been present for 3 days and is not clearly related to activity. No recent medication changes. Sertraline is taken as prescribed; no alcohol or stimulant excess reported.

Office ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without acute ST-T abnormalities. Cardiac examination is regular, without murmur, rub, or gallop. Lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema. Symptoms and examination are reassuring against an acute cardiac process, though ambulatory monitoring is reasonable to exclude an intermittent arrhythmia.

Assessment:
1. Palpitations, likely exacerbated by anxiety.
2. Generalized anxiety disorder with persistent worry, poor sleep, and muscle tension.
3. Atypical chest discomfort.

Plan:
A 7-day ambulatory monitor was ordered. Continue sertraline at the current dose and follow up with primary care for anxiety and sleep management; counseling or cognitive behavioral therapy was encouraged. Limit caffeine and maintain hydration. Seek emergency care for sustained chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or palpitations lasting more than 20 minutes. Return to cardiology after monitor results are available.

- Continue activity as tolerated and rise slowly from sitting or lying down.
- Return to the ED for fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, black or bloody stools, worsening weakness, or inability to keep fluids down.
- Primary-care follow-up for laboratory review and determination of ongoing iron replacement needs.

Patient and friend verbalized understanding of the plan. No medication changes other than continuing ferrous sulfate.

Full PFTs with lung volumes and DLCO.

Collection/report date: 01/07/2022
Reporting laboratory: WOOD COUNTY HOSPITAL
Ordering clinician: Not provided

Clinical indication:
Predictive testing requested because of significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer and ongoing cancer-risk concern. A sibling’s previously documented familial variant was provided for targeted analysis.

Specimen:
Peripheral blood, EDTA whole blood. DNA extraction and quality assessment completed; specimen adequate for testing.

Test performed:
Targeted sequence analysis for the familial BRCA1 variant, BRCA1 c.68_69delAG.

Results:
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: Not detected.

Analytic interpretation:
The tested familial BRCA1 variant was not identified in the submitted specimen. This result substantially reduces the likelihood that the patient carries this specific familial variant, provided the reported familial variant is correct and the specimen is representative. The assay does not exclude other pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, or additional hereditary cancer susceptibility genes.

Clinical interpretation:
Negative targeted testing is most informative when the familial pathogenic variant has been definitively established in an affected relative. Residual risk should be assessed using the complete pedigree, including tumor diagnoses and ages at diagnosis, and may differ from population risk. Genetic counseling is recommended to review limitations, confirm the familial result, and determine whether broader multigene testing is appropriate.

No current treatment is reported.
